questions.problem:
A smartphone app monitors the number of new subscribers, $S(t)$, in thousands, each day since its launch. The following table shows the rate at which new subscriptions are arriving.

| **$t\,\text{(days)}$** | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${S}^{′}(t)\,\text{(thousands/day)}$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ | $2$ | $5.5$ |

$$

$$

At the time $t=6,$ the app had $4$ thousand subscribers. Use the tangent line approximation of $S$ at time $t=6$ to approximate the number of subscriptions at $t=7.$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $S(t)$ at the point $a=6$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =S(a)+{S}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =S(6)+{S}^{′}(6)(t-6) \\  & =4+2(t-6).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $S(7)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $t=7.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}S(7) & ≈L(7) \\  & =4+2(7-6) \\  & =4+2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

An office typist was given the task to transfer all the work documents to the company's internal system. The following table shows some statistics on the process.

| **$t\,\text{(hour)}$** | $4\text{th}$ | $5\text{th}$ | $6\text{th}$ | $7\text{th}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${D}^{′}(t)\,\text{(documents/hour)}$ | $11$ | $8$ | $7$ | $10$ |

$$

$$

The typist transfers the documents at a rate of ${D}^{′}(t)$, where ${D}^{′}(t)$ is measured in documents per hour. At the end of the seventh hour, $t=7$, the typist had completed $50$ documents. Use the tangent line approximation of $D$ at time $t=7$ to determine the number of documents transferred after the ninth hour.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $D(t)$ at the point $a=7$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =D(a)+{D}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =D(7)+{D}^{′}(7)(t-7) \\  & =50+10(t-7).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $D(9)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $t=9.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}D(9) & ≈L(9) \\  & =50+10(9-7) \\  & =50+10(2) \\  & =50+20 \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =d(a)+{d}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =d(2)+{d}^{′}(2)(t-2) \\  & =12+(-0.5)(t-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $d(2.4)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $t=2.4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}d(2.4) & ≈L(2.4) \\  & =12+(-0.5)(2.4-2) \\  & =12+(-0.5)(0.4) \\  & =12-0.2 \\  & =11.8.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(1,4)$ and is concave down on the interval $(0,5).$ If ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ estimate the value of $f(0.8)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(1,4),$ so we have $f(1)=4.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =4+(-2)(x-1) \\  & =4-2x+2 \\  & =-2x+6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(0.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=0.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.8) & ≈L(0.8) \\  & =-2(0.8)+6 \\  & =-1.6+6 \\  & =4.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(0,5),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=1,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.

questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(-2,2)$ and is concave up on the interval $(-3,-1).$ If ${f}^{′}(-2)=-1,$ estimate the value of $f(-1.8)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(-2,2),$ so we have $f(-2)=2.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(-2)=-1,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =2+(-1)(x+2) \\  & =2-(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-1.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-1.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.8) & ≈L(-1.8) \\  & =2-(-1.8+2) \\  & =2-0.2 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave up on the interval $(-3,-1),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is below the graph close to $x=-2,$ and therefore we have an underestimate.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Using a Tangent Line Approximation
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose that $f(-2) = 0$ and $f'(-2)=2.$ Estimate the value of $f(-1.8)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =0+2(x+2) \\  & =2(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-1.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-1.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.8) & ≈L(-1.8) \\  & =2(-1.8+2) \\  & =2(0.2) \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Given its Derivative
canonical_examples.problem: Let $g$ be a function such that $g'(x) =\sqrt{x}$ and $g(4) = 3.$ Using the tangent line approximation of $g(x)$ at $x=4,$ estimate the value of $g(3.6).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $g(x)$ at the point $a=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =g(a)+{g}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =g(4)+{g}^{′}(4)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $g(4)=3,$ and since $g'(x)=\sqrt{x},$ then $g'(4)=\sqrt{4}=2.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =3+2(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $g(3.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(3.6) & ≈L(3.6) \\  & =3+2(3.6-4) \\  & =3+2(-0.4) \\  & =3-0.8 \\  & =2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing a Tangent Line Approximation and Classifying it as an Underestimate or Overestimate
canonical_examples.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(-2,-5)$ and is concave down on the interval $(-\infty,0).$ If $f'(-2)=3$, estimate the value of $f(-2.3)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(-2,-5),$ so we have $f(-2)=-5.$ Also, we're told that $f'(-2)=3,$ so we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-5+3(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-2.3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-2.3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2.3) & ≈L(-2.3) \\  & =-5+3(-2.3+2) \\  & =-5+3(-0.3) \\  & =-5-0.9 \\  & =-5.9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-\infty,0)$, the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=-2,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the function $y=f(x)$ below. Suppose we know that $f(2)=5$ and $f'(2)=1.$ Based on this information, how can we approximate the value of $f(2.75)?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14132147/assets/25baabc5d4193a480d09370faa104d34edc14b2aa09759f5976d592a387fb398.png)

First, recall that the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
y-f(a) = f'(a)(x-a).
$$

Solving for $y$ in the above, we get 

$$
y= f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a)
$$

Now, provided that $x$ is close to $a,$ we can assume that $y\approx f(x) ,$ which gives us the approximation

$$
f(x)\approx f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a).
$$

We often represent the tangent line approximation using the notation $L(x),$ as follows:

$$
L(x)= f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a)
$$

In this case, we want the tangent line approximation at $a=2.$ Substituting this value along with the given information, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2) \\  & =(5)+(1)(x-2) \\  & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's take a look at the graphs. Notice that in the neighborhood of $x=2$, the function and its tangent line approximation are very close. The line $L(x)$ is a good approximation of the function for points close to $x=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14132147/assets/c1de31c316c019e8faf466f64a0e6ff24a29935a7ec354c2acdf18d3069b8d47.png)

As we can see, ${\color{blue}L(2.75)}$ and ${\color{red}f(2.75)}$ are quite close. So, we can approximate $f(2.75)$ using $L(2.75)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.75) & ≈L(2.75) \\  & =(2.75)+3 \\  & =5.75.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent line approximation

$$
L(x)= f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a)
$$

is sometimes also called the **linear approximation** of the function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a.$ The process of approximating the function by its tangent is called **linearization.**

tutorials.name: Underestimate and Overestimate Approximations
tutorials.problem:
Let $L(x)$ be the tangent line approximation of $y = f(x)$ at $x=a,$ as shown in the pictures below. 

| ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14132147/assets/ad7375c544eed881d96d07b449d9003c7df813bdddcdaf29e82bfda6bd4cb283.png) | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14132147/assets/b5b3cd71da3243a5848021831403adde07f1487ff1077f3359d2564ba0f4b686.png) |
| --- | --- |

We can make the following conclusions:

- When the function is *concave up*, the tangent line is *below* the graph (see the picture on the left). Then, 

$$
L(x) \lt f(x)
$$

near $x=a,$ and we say that $L(x)$ gives an *underestimate* of the function.

- When the function is *concave down*, the tangent line is *above* the graph (see the picture on the right). Then, 

$$
L(x) \gt f(x)
$$

near $x=a,$ and we say that $L(x)$ gives an *overestimate* of the function.
